name: KB HOME

priced.reason: not a repriceable fcff name or no growth supplied

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: That I am dismissing the largest gap in today's ten — +211.7% at the 94th percentile of 128 Consumer Discretionary peers — on a data objection for the second time in nine sessions, on a name at 0.76x tangible book with no goodwill, and that the objection is smaller than I claim. The specific form: the $2.11 billion of notes payable I am adding to enterprise value is not corporate leverage in the way a manufacturer's is. It funds $5.98 billion of inventory — land, land under development and homes under construction — which is self-liquidating working capital that converts to cash as houses close. Treating it as permanent debt against a cash-flow stream double-counts, because that same inventory is what produces the deliveries the cash flow comes from. On that reading enterprise value is nearer market capitalisation, the engine's -18.6% implied growth is closer to right than my +2% to +11%, and a builder priced for a 19% five-year cash-flow decline at 0.76x book is exactly what this screen exists to find.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Whether KB Home's debt behaves as working capital — i.e. falls when deliveries fall — or as permanent structural leverage that stays outstanding through the cycle.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Yes, and it defeats the counter on the facts. Deliveries fell 19% and revenue 20% in the quarter, and notes payable went UP, from $1.69 billion to $2.11 billion, 'reflecting cash borrowings outstanding under the Credit Facility'. Debt-to-capital rose 540 basis points to 35.7%. Inventory rose 5% to $5.98 billion while the business shrank a fifth, and $50 million of stock was repurchased in the quarter. That is not self-liquidating working capital unwinding with volumes — it is a company borrowing to hold land and retire shares through a downturn, which is exactly the behaviour that makes debt structural. The debt belongs in enterprise value. The counter does not survive, but it is not worthless either: at 0.76x book with equity of $3.80 billion, an inventory-liquidation scenario genuinely would release cash, and that optionality is part of why the answer is no_edge rather than rich.
devils_advocate.unresolved: The rate path, which is the entire thesis in both directions and which I have no edge on. Also unresolved: what KB Home earns through a normalised cycle. It earned an 11% return on equity in fiscal 2025 and is earning 5% now; whether the through-cycle figure is 8% or 12% decides whether 0.76x book is cheap, and three quarters of a downturn does not answer it.

what_changed: Third-quarter fiscal 2026 results, reported after the close on 2026-09-22 — the settling observable the 2026-09-14 pass on this name explicitly could not test, and it is genuinely mixed. Negative: revenue -20% to $1.30 billion, deliveries -19% to 2,732, homebuilding operating margin 5.2% against 8.1%, net income $65.3 million against $109.8 million, net orders -12% to 2,604, cancellation rate 18% against 17%, full-year revenue guidance about 2% below consensus, and notes payable up to $2.11 billion with debt-to-capital at 35.7%. Positive and genuinely new: ENDING BACKLOG ROSE FOR THE FIRST TIME IN FOUR YEARS — homes in backlog +2% to 4,398 and backlog value +3% to $2.05 billion — average community count +8% to 279, and the Q4 housing gross margin guide of 16.0-16.6% sits at or above the 16.0-16.2% full-year figure, so margin is stabilising rather than continuing to fall. Q3 EPS of $1.05 beat consensus by 19%. The stock fell on the print; the $47.86 in this brief is the 2026-09-22 close and therefore PRE-reaction.
consensus_case: At $47.86 KB Home trades at roughly 0.76x a book value of about $62.80 a share, and the market is pricing the rate environment rather than mispricing the company. Fiscal 2026 is guided to $4.90-5.10 billion of housing revenue against $6.24 billion delivered in fiscal 2025 — deliveries down to 10,500-11,000 — with a housing gross margin of 16.0-16.2% and SG&A of 11.5-11.7%, i.e. a homebuilding operating margin around 4.5% and full-year net income near $190 million on $3.80 billion of equity. That is a 5% return on book. The Federal Reserve HIKED in September 2026, the 30-year mortgage rate is at 7%, and a builder's margin is the first thing incentives and rate buydowns consume. Meanwhile notes payable have risen to $2.11 billion from $1.69 billion a year ago and the debt-to-capital ratio to 35.7% from 30.3%, so the company is levering into the downturn to hold community count and buy back stock. 0.76x book for a 5% return is not a discount; it is arithmetic.
base_case_rationale: Zero to low single digits, and I am deliberately not leaning on the number because the model this feeds cannot price this company (see below). For a homebuilder, CFO less capex is not owner earnings at all: land and inventory investment runs through operating activities, so reported operating cash flow is large and positive when the builder is liquidating and negative when it is growing. The engine's $552.6 million base is the mean of [$335.7M, $362.7M, $1,082.7M] and the $1.08 billion year is the 2023 inventory-liquidation year, which is why the `possible_trough_cycle_base` flag is pointing backwards. A defensible owner-earnings figure is fiscal 2026 net income of roughly $190 million plus the after-tax interest KB Home capitalises into inventory, about $80 million, so roughly $270 million. Against that the business grows if rates fall and shrinks if they do not; backlog turning up and community count +5-8% support flat to slightly positive, and 7% mortgages with the Fed hiking cap it there.
key_risks: The Fed HIKED in September 2026 and the 30-year mortgage rate is at 7%; a homebuilder's gross margin is the first casualty of rate buydowns
Notes payable rose to $2.11B from $1.69B and debt-to-capital to 35.7% from 30.3% while revenue fell 20% — leverage is rising into the downturn
Land optioned at 2024-25 prices is an impairment risk if incentives widen further; Q3 already carried $3.0M of inventory-related charges
Net orders -12% and cancellation rate 18% mean the backlog inflection is not yet demand recovery
NO FAIR VALUE IS RECORDED FOR THIS NAME, deliberately — the engine's enterprise value omits $2.11B of disclosed debt and any number priced through it would be misleading
watch_for: Q4 fiscal 2026 (reporting January 2027): whether housing gross margin lands in the guided 16.0-16.6% or below it
Net orders turning positive, which would convert the backlog inflection into a demand signal
Whether the 30-year mortgage rate breaks back below 6.5%
Notes payable and debt-to-capital: further increases through a shrinking revenue base
